level.title: Compute & Virtual Machines
level.description: Spin up, configure, and optimize virtual machines — the backbone of cloud infrastructure that powers everything from web servers to GPU training clusters.

lessons.title: EC2, Compute Engine & Azure VMs
lessons.content_md:
# EC2, Compute Engine & Azure VMs

Virtual Machines (VMs) are the workhorse of cloud computing. Every major provider offers on-demand, remotely accessible VMs that you can launch in seconds.

## Core Concepts

A cloud VM is a software-emulated computer running on shared physical hardware. You get:
- A virtual CPU (vCPU)
- RAM
- Storage (ephemeral or persistent)
- A network interface with an IP address
- An operating system of your choice

## Provider Comparison

| Feature | AWS EC2 | GCP Compute Engine | Azure VMs |
|---------|---------|-------------------|----------|
| Launch time | ~60s | ~30s | ~60s |
| Custom machine types | No (fixed families) | Yes (any vCPU/RAM combo) | Limited |
| Live migration | Limited | Yes (default) | Yes |
| GPU support | P4, G5, Inf2 | A100, T4, L4 | A100, T4 |
| Free tier | t2.micro (750h/mo) | e2-micro (always free) | B1s (750h/mo) |

## Instance Families

Providers organize VMs into families optimized for different workloads:

| Family | Optimized For | Example Use Case |
|--------|--------------|------------------|
| General Purpose | Balanced CPU/RAM | Web servers, dev environments |
| Compute Optimized | High CPU | Batch processing, gaming servers |
| Memory Optimized | High RAM | In-memory databases, caching |
| Storage Optimized | High I/O | Data warehouses, log processing |
| Accelerated (GPU) | ML/Graphics | Model training, video rendering |

## Launching an EC2 Instance (CLI)

```bash
# Launch a t3.micro instance with Amazon Linux 2
aws ec2 run-instances \
  --image-id ami-0c55b159cbfafe1f0 \
  --instance-type t3.micro \
  --key-name my-key-pair \
  --security-group-ids sg-abc123 \
  --subnet-id subnet-xyz789 \
  --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=instance,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=MyServer}]'
```

## Launching on GCP (gcloud)

```bash
gcloud compute instances create my-server \
  --zone=us-central1-a \
  --machine-type=e2-medium \
  --image-family=ubuntu-2204-lts \
  --image-project=ubuntu-os-cloud \
  --boot-disk-size=20GB
```

## Key Takeaway

Choosing the right instance type is an art. Over-provisioning wastes money; under-provisioning causes outages. Start small, monitor metrics, and right-size iteratively.

lessons.title: AMIs, Images & Machine Templates
lessons.content_md:
# AMIs, Images & Machine Templates

Every VM boots from a **machine image** — a snapshot of an operating system plus any pre-installed software. Understanding images is key to reproducible infrastructure.

## What's in an Image?

```
Machine Image
├── Operating System (Ubuntu, Amazon Linux, Windows)
├── Pre-installed packages (Python, Docker, NGINX)
├── Configuration files
├── Application code (optional)
└── Boot scripts
```

## Provider Terminology

| Provider | Term | Example |
|----------|------|---------|
| AWS | AMI (Amazon Machine Image) | ami-0c55b159cbfafe1f0 |
| GCP | Image / Image Family | ubuntu-2204-lts |
| Azure | VM Image / Shared Image Gallery | Canonical:UbuntuServer:22.04 |

## Using Public Images

All providers maintain catalogs of official, pre-built images:

```bash
# AWS: Find the latest Amazon Linux 2 AMI
aws ec2 describe-images \
  --owners amazon \
  --filters 'Name=name,Values=amzn2-ami-hvm-*-x86_64-gp2' \
  --query 'sort_by(Images,&CreationDate)[-1].ImageId' \
  --output text

# GCP: List available image families
gcloud compute images list --filter="family:ubuntu"
```

## Creating Custom Images

The real power is building your own images with your stack pre-installed:

```bash
# AWS: Create AMI from a running instance
aws ec2 create-image \
  --instance-id i-abc123 \
  --name "my-app-v2.1" \
  --description "Python 3.11 + NGINX + App Code"

# GCP: Create image from a disk
gcloud compute images create my-app-image \
  --source-disk=my-instance \
  --source-disk-zone=us-central1-a
```

## The Golden Image Pattern

```
1. Launch base OS image
2. Install all dependencies (packages, runtimes, agents)
3. Harden security (disable root, configure firewall)
4. Test thoroughly
5. Create image snapshot → "Golden Image"
6. All future instances launch from this image
```

**Benefits:**
- Consistent environments across dev, staging, production
- Faster boot times (no install scripts needed)
- Reduced configuration drift

## Image Builders

For production, automate image creation:

| Tool | Provider |
|------|----------|
| Packer (HashiCorp) | Multi-cloud |
| EC2 Image Builder | AWS |
| Cloud Build | GCP |

```hcl
# Packer template (simplified)
source "amazon-ebs" "base" {
  ami_name      = "my-app-{{timestamp}}"
  instance_type = "t3.micro"
  source_ami    = "ami-0c55b159cbfafe1f0"
}

build {
  provisioner "shell" {
    inline = [
      "sudo apt-get update",
      "sudo apt-get install -y python3 nginx"
    ]
  }
}
```

lessons.title: Pricing Models: On-Demand, Reserved & Spot
lessons.content_md:
# Pricing Models: On-Demand, Reserved & Spot

Compute is typically the largest line item on a cloud bill. Understanding pricing models can save 60-90% on your infrastructure costs.

## On-Demand Instances

Pay by the second (or hour) with no commitment.

```
Cost = hours_running × hourly_rate
```

| Instance | On-Demand/hr (us-east-1) |
|----------|-------------------------|
| t3.micro | $0.0104 |
| m5.large | $0.096 |
| c5.2xlarge | $0.340 |
| p3.2xlarge (GPU) | $3.06 |

**Best for:** Development, unpredictable workloads, short-lived tasks.

## Reserved Instances / Committed Use

Commit to 1 or 3 years in exchange for significant discounts.

| Commitment | Discount vs On-Demand |
|------------|----------------------|
| 1 year, no upfront | ~30-40% |
| 1 year, all upfront | ~40-50% |
| 3 year, all upfront | ~60-72% |

```bash
# AWS: Purchase a reserved instance
aws ec2 purchase-reserved-instances-offering \
  --reserved-instances-offering-id offering-id \
  --instance-count 1
```

**Best for:** Steady-state production workloads that run 24/7.

## Spot Instances (Preemptible VMs)

Use **spare cloud capacity** at massive discounts — but the provider can reclaim your instance with 2 minutes notice.

| Provider | Term | Discount |
|----------|------|----------|
| AWS | Spot Instances | Up to 90% off |
| GCP | Preemptible / Spot VMs | Up to 91% off |
| Azure | Spot VMs | Up to 90% off |

```bash
# AWS: Request a spot instance
aws ec2 run-instances \
  --instance-type c5.xlarge \
  --instance-market-options 'MarketType=spot,SpotOptions={MaxPrice=0.08}'
```

**Best for:** Batch processing, CI/CD, ML training, fault-tolerant workloads.

**Not suitable for:** Databases, user-facing servers, anything that can't handle interruption.

## Cost Optimization Strategies

| Strategy | Savings | Effort |
|----------|---------|--------|
| Right-size instances | 20-40% | Low |
| Spot for batch jobs | 60-90% | Medium |
| Reserved for baseline | 30-72% | Low |
| Schedule dev instances off at night | 65% | Low |
| Use ARM instances (Graviton/Tau) | 20-40% | Low |

## The Hybrid Approach

```
Production baseline:  Reserved Instances (predictable cost)
Peak traffic:         On-Demand Auto Scaling (handles spikes)
Batch processing:     Spot Instances (massive savings)
Dev/Test:             Spot + scheduled stop (minimal waste)
```

This combination typically reduces compute costs by 50-70% compared to pure on-demand.

lessons.title: Hands-On: SSH into a Cloud Server
lessons.content_md:
# Hands-On: SSH into a Cloud Server

Let's connect to a remote cloud server — the most fundamental skill in cloud operations.

## Step 1: Generate an SSH Key Pair

SSH keys replace passwords with cryptographic authentication. You get a **private key** (keep secret) and a **public key** (upload to the cloud).

```bash
# Generate an Ed25519 key pair (modern, secure)
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your_email@example.com"

# You'll get two files:
# ~/.ssh/id_ed25519       ← Private key (NEVER share)
# ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub   ← Public key (upload to cloud)
```

## Step 2: Upload Your Public Key

```bash
# AWS: Import key pair
aws ec2 import-key-pair \
  --key-name my-key \
  --public-key-material fileb://~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

# GCP: Add to project metadata
gcloud compute project-info add-metadata \
  --metadata-from-file ssh-keys=~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
```

## Step 3: Connect via SSH

```bash
# Basic SSH connection
ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 ubuntu@<PUBLIC_IP>

# GCP shortcut (handles keys automatically)
gcloud compute ssh my-instance --zone=us-central1-a

# AWS Systems Manager (no SSH key needed)
aws ssm start-session --target i-abc123
```

## Step 4: Secure Your Connection

### SSH Config File (~/.ssh/config)

Avoid typing long commands every time:

```
Host my-server
  HostName 54.123.45.67
  User ubuntu
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
  Port 22
  ServerAliveInterval 60
```

Now just type: `ssh my-server`

## Common Operations Once Connected

```bash
# Check system resources
free -h              # Memory
df -h                # Disk space
nproc                # CPU cores
uname -a             # Kernel info

# Install software
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y nginx

# Check running services
systemctl status nginx

# View logs
sudo journalctl -u nginx -f

# Transfer files (from your local machine)
scp -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 ./app.tar.gz ubuntu@54.123.45.67:~/
```

## Security Best Practices

| Practice | Why |
|----------|-----|
| Disable password auth | Prevents brute-force attacks |
| Use key-based auth only | Cryptographically secure |
| Change default SSH port | Reduces automated scanning |
| Use a bastion/jump host | Single entry point to private network |
| Enable fail2ban | Auto-blocks repeated failed logins |
| Keep OS updated | Patches known vulnerabilities |

```bash
# Disable password auth in sshd_config
sudo sed -i 's/PasswordAuthentication yes/PasswordAuthentication no/' /etc/ssh/sshd_config
sudo systemctl restart sshd
```

## Windows: RDP Access

For Windows VMs, use Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) on port 3389 instead of SSH. The cloud console provides a password or RDP file for connection.
